## Identifying the correct reservation
3. Do NOT default to the first-listed reservation id — confirm it is the one the user means before writing to it.

-When updating passengers, keep the SAME number of passengers the reservation already has (the passenger count can never change); do not duplicate a passenger to pad the list, or `update_reservation_passengers` will reject the call.
+Match by CITY, not just by airport code. A user names a city; a reservation stores an airport code. One city can have several airports — treat any of a city's airports as a match for that city:
+- New York → EWR, JFK, LGA
+- Chicago → ORD (and MDW)
+- Washington → IAD, DCA
+- Houston → IAH, HOU

+If exactly ONE of the user's reservations matches the cities the user described (even when the stored airport code or date differs from what you expected), that IS the reservation — use it. Never transfer to a human, and never fall back to the first-listed reservation, while a unique city-level match exists.

+When updating passengers, keep the SAME number of passengers the reservation already has (the passenger count can never change); do not duplicate a passenger to pad the list, or `modify_reservation` will reject the call. ## Domain Basic
- If the user doesn't know their reservation id, the agent should help locate it using available tools.

+**All modifications to an existing reservation go through ONE tool: `modify_reservation`.** It changes the cabin, the flight segments, the passenger details, and/or the baggage count — any one of these or several at once. Pass only the arguments for what is changing; leave the rest null. The tool recomputes every price and paid-bag count for you, so you never compute those.
